rv.q: In the hands of playwright Douglas Carter Beane, a quite fine one actually.

Rodgers & Hammerstein's (and Beane's and Brokaw's) Cinderella is as solidly entertaining a commercial proposition as they come, featuring one of Broadway's finest ensembles and what might be its couple of the year.
Reworked for Broadway from its bones as an original 1957 television musical, Rodgers & Hammerstein's Cinderella gets off to a halting start and takes some questionable detours.
Perhaps one could embrace all of this revisionism if it all were lighter and more charming than is the case here.

But with guidance from director Mark Brokaw and librettist Douglas Carter Beane, Osnes and a gifted supporting cast make this fairy tale very much their own -- a scrumptious trifle that, for all its hokey moments, will charm theatergoers of all ages.
This new Broadway production of Rodgers + Hammerstein's Cinderella is a sumptuous, family-friendly spectacle that succeeds in bringing fresh life to the beloved musical.
Luckily, there are some fairy godmothers behind the scenes who redeem this production.
Carroll brings some unintended drama to the fore when asked to dance.
The result is an unwieldy but crowd pleasing concoction that ends up being reasonably entertaining despite its jarring multiple tones.

cn.t: Beane's contemporary revisions inject social consciousness and humor into this visually sumptuous production, though critics split on whether modern touches enhance or undermine the classic's magic.

vs.sum: The Broadway Theatre's vast size (1,761 seats) and exceptional depth mean rear orchestra and balcony seats are very far from the stage, making it best suited to large-scale spectacle productions. The Renaissance-inspired interior is grand, though comfort is below average with tight seating.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Infrared devices available.
